en: The Philippine Eagle, our national bird, hunts monkeys and builds massive nests in tall dipterocarp forest canopies.
Our national flower, the sampaguita, releases its strongest sweet fragrance at night to attract moth pollinators.
The narra, our national tree, sheds its compound leaves during the dry season to survive without rain.
Ifugao farmers carve the Banaue Rice Terraces into mountains, using stone walls to hold soil and flowing water.
During the Pahiyas Festival, Lucban locals decorate homes with kiping, which are dyed rice paste shaped like leaves.
National Scientist Angel Alcala established marine protected areas in Apo Island to help coral reefs and fish recover.
The carabao, our national animal, wallows in mud to cool its body because it lacks sweat glands.
The amihan monsoon brings cool northeast winds, while the habagat monsoon brings heavy rain from the southwest ocean.
The bangus, our national fish, thrives in brackish fishponds where freshwater from rivers mixes with salty seawater.
The South Sea pearl, our national gem, forms inside a large oyster when a tiny sand irritant enters.
T'boli weavers extract strong fibers from abaca plant stalks to weave their traditional, dream-inspired t'nalak cloth.
The anahaw, our national leaf, features large, fan-shaped green fronds that grow in a circular pattern on palms.
